claims.text: The initial magnetic high-entropy alloy has a random solid-solution microstructure.
The initial alloy exhibits moderate coercivity.
A controlled heat treatment or other suitable process can induce nanoscale precipitate formation in the alloy.
Formation of the nanoscale precipitates creates a dual-phase microstructure.
The engineered precipitates will be uniformly distributed at the nanoscale.
Uniform nanoscale precipitates act as domain-wall pinning centers.
Pinning by the precipitates inhibits domain-wall motion.
Inhibition of domain-wall motion increases the coercive field.
The precipitate-containing alloy will have a measurably higher coercive field than a composition-matched random-solid-solution baseline without engineered precipitates.
The coercivity increase is expected at room temperature and atmospheric pressure under standard VSM or SQUID characterization conditions.
The expected effect depends on reproducibly producing the targeted precipitate size and distribution.
Processing deviations that prevent uniform precipitate formation may fail to increase coercivity.
Domain-wall pinning by precipitates is a well-established principle.
The processing window and magnitude of coercivity enhancement for the specific alloys remain undetermined.
Coercivity will be compared between identically composed heat-treated and random-solid-solution control samples using magnetic hysteresis measurements.
TEM or SEM will be used to assess the presence and uniformity of nanoscale precipitates.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that failure to form uniform precipitates may simply prevent the expected effect, whereas the falsification rule treats failure to confirm those precipitates as falsification. Failure of the intervention does not by itself falsify the proposed precipitate-mediated mechanism.
